'''Stefan Cohn-Vossen'''  (28 May 1902 – 25 June 1936) was a [[mathematician]], specializing in [[differential geometry]].
He is best known for his collaboration with [[David Hilbert]] on the 1932 book ''Anschauliche Geometrie'', translated into [[English language|English]] as ''[[Geometry and the Imagination]]''.<ref>{{cite book
  |author1=Hilbert, David
  |author-link=David Hilbert
  |author2=Cohn-Vossen, Stephan
 |title = Geometry and the Imagination |url=https://archive.org/details/geometryimaginat00davi_0|url-access=registration| edition = 2nd
  | year = 1952
  | publisher = Chelsea
  | isbn = 0-8284-1087-9}}
</ref> Both [[Cohn-Vossen's inequality]] and the [[Cohn-Vossen transformation]] are named after him.<ref>{{SpringerEOM| title=Cohn-Vossen transformation | id=Cohn-Vossen_transformation | oldid=16863 | first=M.I. | last=Voitsekhovskii }}</ref> He also proved the first version of the [[splitting theorem]].

== Biography ==
Stefan Cohn-Vossen was born 28 May, 1902 to Emanuel Cohn, a lawyer, and Hedwig (née Vossen) in [[Breslau]] (then a city in the [[Kingdom of Prussia]]; now [[Wrocław]] in [[Poland]]). He attended [[Göttingen University|Göttingen]] in 1920; his notes from Hilbert's lectures on geometry at that time would form the basis for ''Anschauliche Geometrie''.
He wrote a 1924 doctoral dissertation at the [[University of Breslau]] (now the [[University of Wrocław]]) under the supervision of [[Adolf Kneser]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=52164}}</ref> In 1929 he completed his [[habilitation]] at Göttingen with his thesis ''Non-rigid closed surfaces''{{sfn|Cohn-Vossen|1930}} under [[Richard Courant]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Universität zu Köln - Stefan Cohn-Vossen |url=https://professorenkatalog.uni-koeln.de/person/show/143}}</ref>

Cohn-Vossen became a professor at the [[University of Cologne]] in 1930.<ref>{{citation |title=Stefan Cohn-Vossen - Erinnerungskolloquium |date=7 November 2014 |location=Universität zu Köln |url=https://www.mi.uni-koeln.de/Geschichte/COHN-VOSSEN,Stefan/docs/Joint_Presentation_Cohn-Vossen.pdf |ref={{harvid|Stefan Cohn-Vossen, Erinnerungskolloquium 2014}}}}</ref> In 1931, Cohn-Vossen married Dr. Margot Maria Elfriede Ranft. ''Anschauliche Geometrie'' was published in 1932; the book was well reviewed<ref>{{citation |author=Herbert Turnbull |author-link=Herbert Turnbull |title=Review of ''Anschauliche Geometrie'' |journal=Mathematical Gazette |volume=17 |number=225 |year=1933 |pages=277-280}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=MacTutor - Reviews of David Hilbert's books |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Extras/Hilbert_books/#5}}</ref> and by association with Hilbert, Cohn-Vossen became well known.<ref>{{cite web |title=MacTutor - Stefan Emmanuilovich Cohn-Vossen |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Cohn-Vossen/}}</ref>
He was barred from lecturing in 1933 under [[Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service|Nazi racial legislation]], because he was [[Jew]]ish.<ref name="ss">{{citation|title=Mathematicians Fleeing from Nazi Germany: Individual Fates and Global Impact|first=Reinhard|last=Siegmund-Schultze|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2009|isbn=9780691140414|pages=132, 133, 346, 370, 373, 399}}.</ref>

Unable to work in Germany, Cohn-Vossen moved to Switzerland in 1934, first to [[Locarno]] and then to [[Zurich]], where he taught [[gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]]. His son, {{ill|Richard Cohn-Vossen|de|Richard Cohn-Vossen}}, was born in Zurich in September 1934. Both Courant and [[Karl Löwner]] recommended Cohn-Vossen for positions abroad, at [[Istanbul University|Istanbul]] and [[Dartmouth College|Dartmouth]] respectively; ultimately he emigrated to the [[USSR]], with support from [[Herman Müntz]], [[Fritz Houtermans]], [[Pavel Alexandrov]], and [[Heinz Hopf]],<ref>{{harvnb|Siegmund-Schultze|2009}} (p.133) quotes from a 1937 letter by Müntz: "The appointments of Cohn-Vossen, Walfisz, Pollaczek (the latter was not allowed to slip in again) were immediately influenced by myself, the ones for Plessner and Bergmann indirectly."</ref> where he was appointed to the [[Academy of Sciences of the Soviet Union|Academy of Sciences]] and worked at [[Leningrad State University]] and the [[Steklov Institute]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Pasha Zusmanovich |title=Mathematicians going East |journal=Journal of Humanistic Mathematics |volume=14 |number=1 |year=2024 |arxiv=1805.00242}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author-last=Alexandrov |author-first=A.D. |author-link=Aleksandr Aleksandrov (mathematician) |title=On the works of S.E. Cohn-Vossen |journal=[[Uspekhi Matematicheskikh Nauk]] |volume=3 |number=19 |year=1947 }}</ref> 

Cohn-Vossen died in [[Moscow]] from [[pneumonia]] in 1936.<ref>[http://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=rm&paperid=5943&volume=1&year=1936&issue=1&fpage=5&what=fullt&option_lang=rus Cohn-Vossen's Obituary] (in [[Russian language|Russian]])</ref> Despite his short time in the USSR, Cohn-Vossen had a significant impact on the development of differential geometry "in the large"<ref>{{SpringerEOM| title=Geometry in the large | id=Geometry_in_the_large | oldid=24455 }}</ref> in Soviet mathematics.{{sfn|Alexandrov|1947}}<ref>{{cite book| author=N.V. Efimov |author-link=Nikolai Efimov |title=Flachenverbiegung im Grossen |year=1957 |publisher=Akadamie |location=Berlin}}</ref>{{sfn|Cohn-Vossen 1959}}

Following Cohn-Vossen's death, his widow, Dr. Elfriede Cohn-Vossen, remarried [[Alfred Kurella]], returned to Germany in 1954, and died in 1957. His son, Richard, became a filmmaker. In 1946, unaware of his death, the University of Cologne offered Cohn-Vossen his professorship back.{{sfn|Stefan Cohn-Vossen, Erinnerungskolloquium 2014}}
